description: The catalogue of bad arguments, grouped by how they go wrong: bad form, wandering off the point, leaning on the wrong kind of appeal, sneaking in assumptions, mistaking cause, misusing evidence, and the mental biases underneath them.

concepts.title: Formal Fallacies
concepts.summary: Arguments that are invalid by their form alone, whatever they're about. If the shape of the reasoning doesn't guarantee the conclusion, no choice of topic can rescue it.

concepts.title: Affirming the Consequent
concepts.summary: If it rained, the street is wet; the street is wet; so it rained. But a hose would do it too. A true if-then only runs one way.

concepts.title: Denying the Antecedent
concepts.summary: If it rained, the street is wet; it didn't rain; so the street is dry. Not so: other things wet streets. The condition being absent tells you nothing about the result.

concepts.title: Undistributed Middle
concepts.summary: All dogs are mammals; all cats are mammals; so all dogs are cats. Sharing a category doesn't make two things the same thing.

concepts.title: Conjunction Fallacy
concepts.summary: Judging that two things together are likelier than one alone. "A bank teller who is also a feminist" cannot be more probable than "a bank teller," yet vivid detail makes it feel so.

concepts.title: Fallacy Fallacy
concepts.summary: Concluding that a claim is false because someone argued for it badly. A poor argument shows that this case wasn't proven, not that the claim is wrong.

concepts.title: Wandering off the Point
concepts.summary: Fallacies that change the subject: they attack the person or a distorted version of the argument, or drag in something beside the point. Each swaps the question that was asked for an easier one.

concepts.title: Ad Hominem
concepts.summary: Attacking the person instead of the argument: "you can't trust his numbers, he's a known liar." Who says something is a reason to check it harder, but it isn't a refutation.

concepts.title: Straw Man
concepts.summary: Misrepresenting someone's position as weaker or sillier, then defeating that instead. "You want some limits on X? So you want to ban X entirely." It wins an argument nobody was having.

concepts.title: Red Herring
concepts.summary: Introducing an irrelevant point to draw attention from the real one. It works because the new topic is often interesting, and the original question quietly goes unanswered.

concepts.title: Tu Quoque
concepts.summary: "You do it too." Pointing out hypocrisy might be fair criticism of the speaker, but it doesn't make what they said any less true.

concepts.title: Whataboutism
concepts.summary: Answering a criticism by raising a different wrong: "What about when they did it?" Other failures may deserve attention too, but they don't change whether this one happened.

concepts.title: Genetic Fallacy
concepts.summary: Judging an idea by its origin rather than its merits. Where a claim came from can tell you how much to check it, but a good idea from a bad source is still good.

concepts.title: Appeals
concepts.summary: Fallacies that lean on something that feels like a reason but isn't: authority, feeling, nature, tradition, novelty, popularity, or what we can't disprove. Each is sometimes a useful clue and never a proof.

concepts.title: Appeal to Authority
concepts.summary: "An expert says so, so it's true." Expertise is good evidence when the expert is speaking in their field and others agree. It fails when the authority is outside their field, or it's the only reason.

concepts.title: Appeal to Emotion
concepts.summary: Using fear, pity, or anger in place of a reason. Feelings can be appropriate to a conclusion, but a strong feeling doesn't make a claim true.

concepts.title: Appeal to Nature
concepts.summary: "It's natural, so it's good" or the reverse. Arsenic and hemlock are natural; vaccines and glasses aren't. Whether something is natural says little about whether it's safe or right.

concepts.title: Appeal to Tradition
concepts.summary: "We've always done it this way." Longevity can signal that something works, but many long-standing practices were mistaken or unjust, and age alone isn't evidence.

concepts.title: Appeal to Novelty
concepts.summary: "It's new, so it's better." Newness says nothing about quality; the mirror image of appeal to tradition, and as easy to sell.

concepts.title: Bandwagon
concepts.summary: "Everyone believes it, so it's true." What many people think is sometimes good evidence, and it has been badly wrong on plenty of things. Popularity is a clue about belief, not about truth.

concepts.title: Appeal to Ignorance
concepts.summary: "No one has proved it false, so it's true." Absence of disproof isn't proof, and it quietly moves the burden of proof onto the doubter.

concepts.title: Appeal to Consequences
concepts.summary: Judging a claim true or false by whether its outcome is good or bad. "That can't be true, it would be terrible." Reality doesn't adjust to what we'd prefer.

concepts.title: Smuggled Assumptions
concepts.summary: Fallacies that assume what they should prove, limit the options unfairly, or shift the terms mid-argument. The problem sits in what the argument takes for granted before it begins.

concepts.title: Begging the Question
concepts.summary: Circular reasoning: the conclusion is already hidden in a premise. "It's true because the book says so, and the book is always right." It goes nowhere, however confidently it's said.

concepts.title: False Dilemma
concepts.summary: Presenting two options as if they were the only ones. "Either you're with us or against us." Most real questions have more than two answers, and the trick is to hide the others.

concepts.title: Loaded Question
concepts.summary: A question with a built-in assumption: "Have you stopped cheating?" Any direct answer accepts the premise, so the honest reply is to challenge the question itself.

concepts.title: No True Scotsman
concepts.summary: Rescuing a claim by redefining the group after a counterexample: "No real Scotsman puts sugar on porridge." It makes the claim unfalsifiable by moving the category's edge.

concepts.title: Moving the Goalposts
concepts.summary: Changing what would count as proof after it's been met. Every time evidence arrives, the standard rises, so nothing could ever be enough.

concepts.title: Equivocation
concepts.summary: Using one word in two senses within an argument. "A feather is light; what is light can't be dark; so a feather can't be dark." The word slips meaning, and the logic slips with it.

concepts.title: False Equivalence
concepts.summary: Treating two things as equal because they share a feature, ignoring the difference in scale or kind. Both may be flawed, but that doesn't make them equally flawed.

concepts.title: Middle Ground
concepts.summary: Assuming the truth lies halfway between two positions. Sometimes a compromise is best, but if one side is simply wrong, splitting the difference builds the error into the answer.

concepts.title: Mistaking Cause
concepts.summary: Fallacies about what causes what: assuming that what follows was caused, that things which move together are linked, or that one small step must lead to disaster.

concepts.title: Post Hoc
concepts.summary: After this, therefore because of this. The rooster crows and the sun rises; the sun does not rise because of the rooster. Coming first isn't the same as causing.

concepts.title: Correlation vs Cause
concepts.summary: Two things rising together may be linked by a third, by chance, or in the opposite direction. Ice cream sales and drownings both climb in summer; neither causes the other.

concepts.title: Single Cause
concepts.summary: Naming one cause for something with many. Wars, recessions, and illnesses rarely have a single reason, and picking one usually says more about the speaker than the event.

concepts.title: Slippery Slope
concepts.summary: Claiming that one step will inevitably lead to a chain of worse ones, without showing each link. Some slopes are real; the fallacy is asserting one without the evidence.

concepts.title: Misusing Evidence
concepts.summary: Fallacies about how evidence is gathered and used: too little, chosen to suit, or ignoring the numbers that matter. They make a conclusion look better supported than it is.

concepts.title: Hasty Generalization
concepts.summary: Drawing a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases. "I met two rude tourists; that country is rude." The sample was too small to say anything about the whole.

concepts.title: Anecdote
concepts.summary: Treating a personal story as proof. "My uncle smoked and lived to ninety." Vivid and memorable, but one case can't outweigh the statistics of thousands.

concepts.title: Cherry Picking
concepts.summary: Showing only the evidence that fits and leaving out what doesn't. Each fact may be true; the picture they add up to is false because of what was left out.

concepts.title: Survivorship Bias
concepts.summary: Studying only what survived a process and missing what didn't. In the war, armor was added where returning bombers were hit, until someone realized the ones hit elsewhere never came back.

concepts.title: Texas Sharpshooter
concepts.summary: Firing at a barn, then painting the target around the bullet holes. Finding a pattern after the fact in noisy data, then treating it as if you'd predicted it.

concepts.title: Gambler's Fallacy
concepts.summary: Believing that after a run of one outcome, the other is "due." A fair coin has no memory: ten heads in a row leaves the next flip at fifty-fifty.

concepts.title: Base Rate Fallacy
concepts.summary: Ignoring how common something is when judging a test result. A 95%-accurate test for a rare disease still gives mostly false alarms, because healthy people vastly outnumber the sick.

concepts.title: Composition and Division
concepts.summary: Assuming what's true of the parts is true of the whole, or the reverse. Every brick is light, so the wall is light; the team is the best, so each player must be. Neither follows.

concepts.title: Cognitive Biases
concepts.summary: Systematic quirks in how minds judge, remember, and decide. They aren't stupidity; they're shortcuts that usually work and sometimes fail in predictable ways, which is why they underlie so many fallacies.

concepts.title: Confirmation Bias
concepts.summary: Seeking, noticing, and remembering evidence that agrees with what we already think. It works quietly in everyone, and is why testing your beliefs means looking for what could prove them wrong.

concepts.title: Anchoring
concepts.summary: Leaning too heavily on the first number or idea we hear. Whoever names a price first shapes the whole negotiation, even when the number was arbitrary.

concepts.title: Availability Heuristic
concepts.summary: Judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Plane crashes and shark attacks feel common because they're vivid, though far ordinary risks are much more likely.

concepts.title: Sunk Cost
concepts.summary: Carrying on with something because of what's already been spent. Money, time, and effort already gone can't be recovered; only what's still ahead should count in the decision.

concepts.title: Hindsight Bias
concepts.summary: After the fact, feeling that it was obvious all along. It makes the past look more predictable than it was, and makes us harsher on decision-makers who had less information than we do now.

concepts.title: Motivated Reasoning
concepts.summary: Reasoning toward the conclusion we want. We scrutinize unwelcome evidence hard and accept welcome evidence easily, all while feeling entirely fair.

concepts.title: Framing Effect
concepts.summary: The same facts land differently depending on how they're put: "90% survive" feels better than "10% die." Noticing the frame is the first step to seeing what's underneath it.

concepts.title: Dunning–Kruger Effect
concepts.summary: People with little skill in an area tend to overrate it, since the skills needed to judge are the skills they lack. How large the effect is remains debated, but the humility it points to is useful.
